title: National Agreement on Closing the Gap (Closing the Gap)
subtitle: National Cabinet (Formerly Council of Australian Governments) · 2020–2031
description:
Closing the Gap is a commitment from all Australian Governments and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander representatives to a fundamentally new way of developing and implementing policies and programs that impact the lives of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people. This includes policies and programs impacting recruitment, health and social programs specific to First Nations peoples, many of which are relevant to the Public Safety and Government industry-sectors.

Closing the Gap is jointly implemented by the Federal, State and Territory governments, along with Australian Local Government Associations and Coalitions of Peaks. It focuses on four priority reforms (strengthen formal partnerships and shared decision making; build the community-controlled sector; transform government organisations; and shared access to data) and 19 national socio-economic targets, covering areas such as life expectancy, education, employment, justice and child protection. Overall progress towards meeting Closing the Gap targets has been mixed. Implementation of Closing the Gap is ongoing to 2031. The Productivity Commission is tracking these targets.
impactDescription: The National Agreement on Closing the Gap has informed the research and engagements undertaken as part of the 2026 Local Government Workforce Insights Report, as it highlights and reaffirms the importance of working toward programs and initiatives that impact First Nations communities. Closing the Gap has informed engagement with Local Government stakeholders, particularly with the First Nations Councils who participated in the Local Government Skills Audit and uptake and utility of the Local Government Training Package project. This has ensured that the policies and programs impacting First Nations peoples, employees, and community members, are reflected accurately and fairly in this Report.

title: The Australian Government's Strategic Priorities
subtitle: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet · 2022-2026
description: The Australian Government's Strategic Priorities provide a four-year (2022-2026) policy direction for the Australian Public Service (APS) and sets targets across key areas. These areas include the economy, public health and climate change. The Australian Government's Strategic Priorities are into the final year of their implementation by the Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet with the relevant APS departments and organisations. So far, the Australian Government's Strategic Priorities have achieved several outcomes, including hosting a Jobs and Skills Summit, developing a plan for cheaper childcare, implementing fee-free TAFE and creating more university places, establishing the National Reconstruction Fund, introducing legislation for a national anti-corruption commission and strengthening strategic partnerships in the Pacific and Southeast Asia. Progress is continuing for public health and aged care; improving housing supply and planning reforms; and advancing government budget sustainability.
impactDescription: The Australian Government Strategic Priorities have provided guidance for the 2026 Local Government Workforce Insights Report, as it clearly identifies where efforts can be made by the Local Government industry-sector, Local Government stakeholders, and Public Skills Australia in working toward shared goals. Specifically, these priorities are relevant to Local Government as they address identified challenges such as housing, TAFE funding and sustainability practices among government.

title: Working for Women — A Strategy for Gender Equality
subtitle: Australian Government – Minister for Women · 2023–ongoing
description:
The Working for Women Strategy outlines a framework for the Australian Government to improve national gender equality. It sets out five priority areas and reports on a range of outcomes and indicators annually to monitor Australia's progress. These priority areas are:
Priority Area 1 - Gender-based violence
Priority Area 2 - Unpaid and paid care
Priority Area 3 - Economic equality and security
Priority Area 4 - Health
Priority Area 5 - Leadership, representation and decision-making

Specific to JSCs, Priority Area 3 focuses on improving gender pay gaps, supporting access to skills and training and reducing occupational and industrial gender segregation. To date, the Australian Government has increased female recruitment into trades and other occupations through apprenticeship support, fee-free TAFE and targets in the Australian Skills Guarantee, along with including gender equality as a national priority in the National Skills Agreement. In March 2025, the Department for Workplace Relations launched the Advancing Gender Equality in Gender Segregated Industries grant program, directly linked to Priority Area 3. This grant program received a $28.5 million extension in December 2025.
impactDescription: The above priorities have informed the contextualisation of research for the 2026 Local Government Workforce Insights Report. Understanding challenges and developing mitigating strategies on key gender equity priorities remains a goal of Public Skills Australia across all research and reporting. Public Skills Australia will continue to prioritise diversity and inclusion in all research and to fairly report employment, skills and training challenges as it relates to gender equality.

title: The Clean Energy Generation: Workforce Needs for a Net Zero Economy
subtitle: Jobs and Skills Australia · 2023–2025
description:
The Clean Energy Generation considers emerging and future clean-energy workforce requirements as Australia strives to reach net-zero emissions by 2050. JSA's preliminary modelling estimates Australia's clean-energy workforce will need to grow from the current 53,000 employees to 84,000 employees by 2050.

The Clean Energy Generation makes 50 recommendations to support Governments in focusing their efforts on how skills shortages can be averted in the set time, resources and legislative constraints and government objectives. Broadly, the recommendations cover the challenge areas of participation and attraction, hiring and retention, transitioning employees and communities, roles and responsibilities, critical occupations, education and training and transport. Implementation remains ongoing and long-term, aligned with the 2050 net-zero target.
impactDescription: The Local-Government industry-sector is exposed to the risks posed by climate change, particularly the increased frequency of environmental crises. This is leading to skills and occupation gaps in emergency management occupations which Public Skills Australia is addressing through The Local Government Emergency Management Skills Project.

title: Australian Cyber Security Strategy
subtitle: Department of Home Affairs · 2023–2030
description:
The 2023–2030 Australian Cyber Security Strategy serves as a roadmap to achieve the Australian Government's vision of becoming a world leader in cyber security by 2030.

The 2023–2030 Australian Cyber Security Strategy is structured around six 'cyber shields' (strong citizens and businesses, safe technology, world-class threat sharing, protected critical infrastructure, sovereign capability and resilient regional/global leadership). These are to be delivered in three stages or 'Horizons' (2023-2025 strengthening the foundations, 2026-2028 scaling efforts across the whole economy and 2029-2030 leading the development of new cyber technologies). Progress to date has focused on the foundational aspects of the Strategy, with the initial work under 'Horizon 1' (2023-2025) concentrating on improving incident reporting and response mechanisms, introducing legislative reforms, piloting threat-sharing initiatives and raising government and critical infrastructure security standards. Overall coordination sits with the Department of Home Affairs, specifically through the Australian Cyber Security Coordinator. The remaining two horizons are to be implemented over the next four years up to 2030.
impactDescription: The 2023–2030 Australian Cyber Security Strategy has informed the 2026 Local Government Workforce Insights Report by outlining priorities for the federal government to maintain Australia's cyber security. This information is highly relevant for the Local Government industry-sector, where cyber security occupations and skills are in shortage.

title: Unlocking the Potential of VET
subtitle: Qualification Reform Design Group · 2024
description:
In March 2024, the Qualification Reform Design Group (QRDG) provided advice to Skills Ministers on reforming the Vocational Education and Training (VET) qualifications system. This included advising that:
Qualification and unit of competency design and development processes should be reviewed and updated where appropriate
The VET system should be consolidated by removing training products that are under-utilised or unnecessarily duplicated
The Training Package Organising Framework should be updated, where necessary

As a result, Public Skills Australia undertook a Demonstration Project that consulted widely to determine the efficacy of updating qualification and unit of competency templates. This Report was delivered to the QRDG in Q3 2024.

In December 2024, the QRDG provided their final report and recommendations to Skills Minsters, based on national consultation and findings from the JSC Demonstration Projects. The recommendations from this Report centred around modernising VET qualifications by implementing a purpose-led, principles-based approach to qualification design. As a result, JSCs are responsible for ensuring qualifications serve a clear purpose, are linked to workforce needs and are not unnecessarily duplicated.
impactDescription: This work has informed Public Skills Australia researching into the utilisation and purpose of the LGA Local Government Training Package. As a result, projects are underway at Public Skills Australia to Review the Uptake and Utility of the LGA Local Government Training Package. This will ensure that training products provided to the Local Government workforces are streamlined, purposeful and relevant to meet the needs of the workforces and address current skills and training challenges.

title: Occupation Standard Classification for Australia
subtitle: Australian Bureau of Statistics · 2024–ongoing
description:
Formally known as Australia New Zealand Standard Classification of Occupation (ANZSCO), the Occupation Standard Classification for Australia (OSCA) is a standardised framework for classifying occupations in Australia. As part of the replacement process from ANZSCO to OSCA in 2024, the ABS announced that OSCA will undergo regular updates in accordance with the OSCA Maintenance Strategy, which was released in 2025.

The changes to OSCA outlined in the Maintenance Strategy involve stakeholder engagement and are timed to ensure that each Census of Population and Housing uses the most recent update. Under the strategy, the first round of consultations and feedback with stakeholders on proposed changes to OSCA are scheduled to be completed in August 2026, with the next update to be published in March 2027 before the data release of the 2026 Census in October 2027.
impactDescription: The OSCA standardised framework is a key data source for Public Skills Australia in all research pertaining to occupations. Public Skills Australia will continue to be involved in providing feedback for the framework, to ensure data release are purposeful to the Public Safety and Administration sector. The 2026 Local Government Workforce Insights Report has utilised the OSCA framework in occupational mapping exercises across the Local Government workforces.

title: 2024 Core Skills Occupation List — Key Findings Report
subtitle: Jobs and Skills Australia · 2024–ongoing
description:
The Core Skills Occupation List (CSOL) provides labour market analysis that informs the identification of occupations that are considered appropriate for employer-sponsored temporary migration through the Core Skills Stream of the Skills in Demand (SID) Visa.

The 2024 CSOL Key Findings Report compiled a list of 456 occupations considered appropriate for the Core Skills Stream of the new employer-sponsored temporary SID visa. In addition to updating the list, JSA examined the drivers of skill shortages through CSOL analysis and stakeholder engagement and identified a 'suitability gap' category - occupations where there are enough qualified applicants, but they are not regarded as suitable by employers (e.g. auditors, electronics engineers, software and applications programmers). JSA also identified a 'retention gap' category - occupations with below-average rates of retention such as construction and hospitality jobs and child carers. JSA's consultations to inform the 2025 CSOL opened in August 2025 and JSA submitted its advice to Government for consideration in October 2025.
impactDescription: The 2024 CSOL Key Findings Report has provided contextual information around appropriate skilled migration pathways through the Local Government industry sector. These types of employment pathways are becoming popular ways for local councils to fill vacant job roles, particularly in regional, rural and remote areas where recruitment pools are limited. Reports such as this are important in understanding barriers to these employment pathways, and how the local council employers can work within the parameters of certain Visas to address occupation needs.

title: Better Together — The Jobs and Skills Report 2024
subtitle: Jobs and Skills Australia · 2024–ongoing
description:
Better Together was released in November 2024 as part of JSA's mandated obligations to provide insight on the Australian labour market and advice on workforce needs and priorities. It details evidence aligned to five strategic pillars to enable a more prosperous economic future, including:
Fostering inclusive participation: Focused on broadening employment opportunities through identifying and removing barriers for people and communities
Understanding today's workforce: Detailing data to build an evidence base that informs and addresses current and emerging labour market and skills needs
Shaping Australia's future workforce: Projecting forward to plan for the opportunities and challenges of Australia's future workforce needs
Optimising pathways and system architecture: Monitoring, analysing and advising on the effectiveness of the Vocational Education and Training (VET) system as key to skilling the workforce
Activating an informed dialogue: Detailing stakeholder engagement across the VET system to provide the best evidence and advice on Australia's current and future workforce and skills needs and opportunities

Better Together outlines JSA's key current and emerging datasets that provide useful insights on the intricacies of Australia's labour market for use in development of strategic workforce planning for the JSCs.
impactDescription: Better Together provided insights for clear goals and initiatives that the Local Government industry-sector can continue work towards. Public Skills Australia carries many of these priorities in our research and engagement with the Local Government industry-sector. These address themes such as diversity and inclusion, First Nations participation, evolving VET landscape, and skills and training challenges, all of which Public Skills Australia aims to address through research and stakeholder engagement within the Local Government industry-sector.

title: Training Package Organising Framework
subtitle: Skills and Workforce Ministerial Council · 2025–ongoing
description: In July 2025, the Training Package Organising Framework (TPOF) was updated based on advice from the QRDG in December 2024. Housing the Training Package Products Development and Endorsement Process Policy (TPPDEPP), Training Package Products Policy (TPPP) and the Standards for Training Packages, the TPOF, sets out the process for developing and seeking approval of new VET training products for JSCs. As a JSC, Public Skills Australia will continue to adhere to the TPOF to ensure the Australian VET system is high-performing and readily supports student and industry needs.
impactDescription: The TPOF Framework is highly relevant to the work being undertaken for the LGA Local Government Training Package with the potential development of new training products being researched at time of publishing the 2026 Local Government Workforce Insights Report. Systems such as the TPOF will ensure accuracy and relevancy for new Local Government training products, that will address skills and training challenges.

title: Five Pillars of Productivity Inquiries — Final Reports
subtitle: Productivity Commission · 2025–ongoing
description:
The Productivity Commission has provided 47 recommendations across 'five pillars' of productivity policy:
Creating a more dynamic and resilient economy
Building a skilled and adaptable workforce
Harnessing data and digital technology
Delivering quality care more efficiently
Investing in cheaper, cleaner energy and the net zero transformation

At the time of drafting this Report, the Australian Government is yet to provide response to the recommendations.
impactDescription: Public Skills Australia follows the advice and recommendations of the Productivity closely, to ensure the research and training products available to the Local Government industry-sector are addressing relevant challenges. Of the five pillars above, building a skilled and adaptable workforce is most relevant to the Local Government workforce. Public Skills Australia will continue to monitor the response to the recommendations, and how this will impact the Local Government industry-sector.

title: Opportunity and Productivity: Towards a Tertiary Harmonisation Roadmap Report
subtitle: Jobs and Skills Australia · 2025–ongoing
description: This Report seeks to articulate the benefits of a deeper harmonised tertiary sector and provides recommendations on how to create a sustainable pathway forward in collaboration with key stakeholders. It outlines 19 key recommendations, across three categories (Enabling the tertiary harmonisation roadmap; Early priorities for the roadmap and medium-term horizon roadmap priorities) to work towards a harmonised system that can tackle national challenges, address skilled workforce shortages and improve productivity.
impactDescription: For the Local Government industry-sector, this report can provide insights for best practice within the tertiary education system, and how these practices compare to the current VET system utilised by the Local Government industry-sector for skills and training needs.

title: Gender Economic Equality Study
subtitle: Jobs and Skills Australia · 2025–ongoing
description:
The Gender Economic Equality Study explored three challenges for the jobs and skills systems that contribute to gender economic inequality:
occupational segregation
pay gaps and gendered divides in the education
training and skills systems

The study was reported over three papers, with the third and final paper Speeding up progress towards gender economic equality being released in October 2025. This paper sets out 10 recommendations to address challenges in the jobs and skills system that perpetuate inequality and impact productivity:
1. Deliver a three-year 'Shifting the Dial on Gender Segregation' action and evaluation agenda
2. Introduce early career learning into schools to intervene earlier in gendered study choices
3. Embed gender targets and reporting across future National Skills Agreements
4. Coordinate national action to reduce gender segregation in VET pathways for shortage occupations
5. Support First Nation women through a standalone economy-wide plan
6. Accelerate inclusive, safe and respectful workplaces and training settings
7. Normalise men's participation in paid and unpaid care work
8. Adopt the Gender Segregation Intensity Scale (GSIS) to guide and measure progress
9. Further address gender bias in labour market and skills frameworks
10. Expand research, data and intersectional analysis to strengthen accountability
impactDescription: These recommendations have been influential in determining future research into the Local Government workforce gender equality priorities. It outlines recommendations with the potential to shape the future of the Local Government workforce toward fairer gender balances, including addressing the gender pay gap, which Public Skills Australia will continue to monitor for future insights.

title: Occupational Shortage List (OSL)
subtitle: Jobs and Skills Australia · Ongoing
description:
The Occupational Shortage List (OSL), formerly the Skills Priority List, offers an annual point-in-time review of the status of Australian occupations. Specifically, the OSL reports on whether occupations (at the 4-digit and 6-digit ANZSCO level, and the 6-digit OSCA level) are experiencing shortages nationally and for each State and Territory in regional or metropolitan areas.

The OSL was last updated in 2025. The latest OSL differed from previous iterations due to the fact that in 2024 the ANZSCO classification framework for occupations was replaced with the OSCA classifications. In terms of the 2025 OSL results, it was reported that 29 per cent of occupations (293 out of 1,022 assessed) were in national shortage, which was 4 per cent lower than 2024 (33 per cent) and more than 7 per cent lower than 2023 (36 per cent). The OSL in 2025 also added 29 occupations newly in shortage compared to 2024, most of which were roles related to health, science, technicians and trades and machinery operators and drivers. As at February 2026, JSA had started the 2026 OSL survey but it had not yet confirmed a publication date for this year's list.
impactDescription: The OSL remains a key data source across Public Skills Australia's work. For the Local Government Skills Audit, the OSL was a crucial tool to assist in identifying relevant Local Government industry-sector occupational shortages.
